idiom_name: typed Iterable<T>/Iterator<T>/IterableIterator<T> over the JS protocol (+ downlevelIteration)
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types, not mechanics: lib.es2015.iterable.d.ts declares Iterable<T> (a [Symbol.iterator](): Iterator<T> member), Iterator<T, TReturn, TNext> with next(value?) plus optional return/throw, IterableIterator<T> for objects that are both, and Generator<T, TReturn, TNext> for generator functions, so a collection can state exactly which protocol it satisfies and the compiler checks for-of, spread and destructuring against it. Runtime behaviour is the JavaScript protocol - the classic two-role structure is still the protocol, just typed - and targeting below ES2015 needs the downlevelIteration flag (plus a Symbol.iterator shim) for non-array iterables, because for-of is otherwise restricted to arrays. Type API parameters as Iterable<T> and keep the concrete iterator private.
pitfalls: With target ES5/ES3, for-of over non-array iterables is a compile error unless downlevelIteration is enabled, and even then the emitted helper needs Symbol.iterator at runtime (a shim); arrays are silently special-cased, so the same loop works and fails depending on the value's static type.

Generator type parameters are subtle: a Generator<T, TReturn, TNext> whose TNext is not undefined is not assignable to IterableIterator<T>, which is why the lib keeps them separate and why older code using IterableIterator may not typecheck against new generators.
Iterable<T> promises nothing about re-iteration: a generator satisfies the type although it is single-use, so an API handed a spent iterator compiles and fails at runtime.

lib and target settings decide which protocol declarations exist (es2015/esnext) and how IteratorReturnResult/BuiltinIteratorReturn are typed, so the same code types differently across compiler configurations.
